Of these reports, certain information has been redacted pursuant to G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (c) as this
information constitutes either medical information or personal and highly intimate details which
if disclosed would constitute an unwarranted invasion of the deceased’s and/or third-parties’
privacy. See G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (c) (“personnel and medical files or information; also any other
materials or data relating to a specifically named individual, the disclosure of which may constitute
an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy”). Third-party civilian names have been withheld at
this time pursuant to G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (f)(investigatory exemption) as disclosure of their identities
would have a chilling effect and discourage “individual citizens to come forward and speak freely
with police concerning matters under investigation.” Bougas v. Chief of Police of Lexington, 371
Mass. 59, 62 (1976). Any references to an underage sexual encounter, which on its face would
appear to constitute statutory rape, have been withheld under G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (a) (“specifically
or by necessary implication exempted from disclosure by statute”); G.L. c. 41, §97D (all reports
of rape and sexual assault or attempts to commit such offenses shall be maintained as confidential).

Also, please find enclosed the redacted Stoughton Police Department internal affairs report, which
was previously released and redacted by the Stoughton Police Department. The unredacted
Stoughton Police Department internal affairs report and associated exhibits have been withheld at
this time pursuant to G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (f)(investigatory exemption) as disclosure of these records
would so jeopardize the NDAO’s criminal investigation that such disclosure is not in the public
interest. See Globe Newspaper Co. v. Police Commr. of Boston, 419 Mass. 852, 859 n.10
(2004)(materials compiled for internal affairs investigation covered by investigatory exemption);
Bougas, 371 Mass. at 62 (purposes of investigatory exemption include “premature disclosure of
the Commonwealth's case prior to trial, the prevention of the disclosure of confidential
investigative techniques, procedures, or sources of information, the encouragement of individual
citizens to come forward and speak freely with police concerning matters under investigation, and
the creation of initiative that police officers might be completely candid in recording their
observations, hypotheses and interim conclusions”).1

The NDAO is in possession of personal messages of the deceased, Sandra Birchmore, which were
procured from her personal cellular phone and laptop. These messages contain highly personal
and intimate details, including sexually explicit content. These messages are also currently subject
to the NDAO’s criminal investigation. Accordingly, these messages have been withheld under the
following statutory exemptions: G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (f) (investigatory exemption) and G.L. c. 4, §
7 (26) (c).

                                                                                   March 8, 2021


                  Sergeant John Fanning

                  State Police Detective Unit

                  45 Shawmut Road. Second Floor

                  Canton, MA 02021


                            Re:     Sandra Birchmore Death Investigation


                  Dear Sgt. Fanning:


                            I am writing to follow-up on our recent conversations and prior interviews you have had

                  with my client. Matthew Farwell.      As you know, Mr. Farwell has been cooperative with your

                  investigation. including participating in interviews with you and permitting you to download

                  certain    formation from his mobile phone.


                            Throughout your conversations with my client, and later with myself, you have indicated

                 that you view him as a witness in your investigation.      This is consistent with reality.   Mr. Farwell

                 has committed no crime.       Like many. he is saddened by Ms. Birchmore's death.


                            During our recent conversations, you asked Mr. Farwell to submit a DNA sample and

                 participate in a polygraph interview.    Although I appreciate your diligence, I advised my client lo

                 decline these requests and the request for further interview (traditional/non-polygraph) that

                 accompanied them.       I did so because they are far outside the norm for mere witnesses in an

                 investigation.    I was a prosecutor for 1 4 years and participated in hundreds of interviews with

                 State Police detectives like yourself.   I cannot recall once seeking a polygraph interview.       And I

                 can only recall seeking I) NA of persons that the investigators and I considered targets.


                            There are good reasons for anyone to chafe at a request for ON A and polygraph and for

                 an attorney to advise his client to decline the request.   Compiling Mr. Farwell's DNA profile

                 would be highly invasive.     It would yield genetic markers and highly personal health and family

                 information.     Based on the information he has already provided to you that I will not restate here.

                 I expect his DNA profile would reveal nothing of value to your case.       Mr. Farwell has already

                 provide highly personal information.       In my opinion. providing DNA is a step too far.
        A polygraph raises similar concerns about invasion of privacy.   The topics of questioning

would be highly invasive.   Furthermore, the results of a polygraph are inadmissible in court

because courts have concluded that polygraph results are unreliable.   See Commonwealth •

Mendes, 406 Mass. 201 (1989).     Under the circumstances here, there is no reason for the State

Police to conduct a polygraph examination of my client.


        I write not only to explain my response to your request for DNA and polygraph ofmy

client, but also to briefly address two points that may be underlying your requests.   First, my

client had no role in Ms. Birchmore's death.   He certainly never encouraged her to take her life,

nor did he have any reason to fear that she would take her own life.   He was shocked and

saddened when he learned that she had taken her own life.


       If possible, please inform me when your investigation closes and of any conclusions (if

any) that you draw with respect to Mr. Farwell.   Please contact me if! may provide additional

assistance to you or if you would like to contact my client.
                                                                                                            SSACHUS

Re: Public Records Request

Dear Mr. Cullinane:

This responds to your November 8, 2022 public records request to the Norfolk District Attorney’s Office
(NDAO) in which you requested under G.L. c. 66, § 10: “Any memos or emails sent or received by any
employee of the Massachusetts State Police from February 1, 2021 to present day which contain the
phrase ‘Birchmore,’ ‘Sandra Birchmore’ or ‘Farwell.’”

The NDAO reasonably reads your request as seeking emails containing the above mentioned phrases, sent
or received by a member of the Massachusetts State Police Detective Unit (SPDU) assigned to the
NDAO.

As you may be aware, on August 29, 2022, Stoughton Police Department concluded its internal
investigation and subsequently released to the public a redacted report of its findings concerning former
Stoughton Police officers Matthew Farwell; William Farwell; and Robert Devine. This Office is
conducting a review of the Stoughton Police Department’s findings and allegations concerning these
individuals. Notwithstanding this Office’s investigation into whether these individuals’ actions constitute
criminal conduct prosecutable by this Office, the NDAO will at this time release the enclosed emails
responsive to your request.

Enclosed please find emails sent or received by members of the SPDU assigned to the NDAO. (91 pages).

Of these records, certain information and graphic depictions of the deceased were redacted pursuant to
G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26)(c) as this information constitutes either medical information or personal and highly
intimate details which if disclosed would constitute an unwarranted invasion of the deceased’s and/or
third-parties’ privacy. See G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26)(c) (“personnel and medical files or information; also any
other materials or data relating to a specifically named individual, the disclosure of which may constitute
an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy”). Emails relating to an inquiry by the Massachusetts Peace
Officer Standards and Training Commission were withheld as they are kept confidential. See G.L. c. 4, §
7 (26)(a); G.L. c. 6E, §8(c)(2). Additionally, emails concerning public record requests involving the
above listed terms were withheld as they contain NDAO internal deliberations, the disclosure of which
could taint the deliberative process. G.L. c. 4 § 7 (26)(d); DaRosa v. City of New Bedford, 471 Mass. 446
(2015).

Furthermore, certain emails pertaining to the active and ongoing criminal investigation are exempt from
public disclosure pursuant to statutory exclusions and contain attorney work product. See G.L. c. 4, § 7
Mr. Cullinane
January 20, 2023
pg. 2

(26)(d); DaRosa, 471 Mass. at 459, 462 (holding that attorney work product is held privileged); G.L. c. 4,
§ 7 (26)(f) (“investigatory materials necessarily compiled out of the public view by law enforcement or
other investigatory officials the disclosure of which materials would probably so prejudice the possibility
of effective law enforcement that such disclosure would not be in the public interest”); See also Globe
Newspaper Co. v. Police Commr. of Boston, 419 Mass. 852, 859 n.10 (2004)(materials compiled for
internal affairs investigation covered by investigatory exemption); Bougas v. Chief of Police of Lexington,
371 Mass. 59, 62 (1976) (purposes of investigatory exemption include “premature disclosure of the
Commonwealth's case prior to trial, the prevention of the disclosure of confidential investigative
techniques, procedures, or sources of information, the encouragement of individual citizens to come
forward and speak freely with police concerning matters under investigation, and the creation of initiative
that police officers might be completely candid in recording their observations, hypotheses and interim
conclusions”).

You have a right to appeal this response in accordance with G.L. c. 66, § 10 and 950 Code Mass. Regs. §
32.08 (2021) to: Supervisor of Public Records, Office of the Secretary of the Commonwealth, Public
Records Division, One Ashburton Place, 17th Floor, Boston, MA 02108.

          Chief McNamara:


                  Pursuant to your directive of February 5, 2021 to conduct this investigation, I hereby


          submit the following report into the matter of the unattended death of Sandra Birchmore, and


          into the possible violations of the policies, procedure, rules and regulations of the Stoughton


          Police Department:


          Investigative directive


                  This administrative investigation was conducted to determine any violations of policies


          procedures, rules and regulations of the Stoughton Police Department by any of its employees.


                  This investigation began as a result of the unattended death investigation that was


          conducted by the Massachusetts State Police into the death of Sandra Birchmore of Canton, MA,


          formerly of Stoughton, MA and a former participant in the Stoughton Police Explorers program.


          Investigative reports and evidence in this case was shared by the Massachusetts State Police


          concerning personal relationships that members of the Stoughton Police Department had with


          Ms. Birchmore.


           I
       Throughout the course of this investigation there was an understanding between the


Massachusetts State Police and me, that should any evidence be discovered concerning criminal


culpability involving anybody connected in any way to this case, that I would refer that


information to the MSP for further investigation.


          Per policy, the Chief of Police received weekly updates as to the progress of this


investigation [Standard 52.2.4] and on occasion, with more frequency when relevant. A


determination was made in the early stages of this investigation that disclosure of allegations to


employees who would eventually be identified, would jeopardize this investigation [Standard


52.2.5]


          An approximate timetable was provided and updated as information developed. Some


delays in the processing of data were beyond the control of this investigator. Any dispositions or


findings are based upon the Preponderance o
                                          fEvidence standard of proof,

Conclusion


        Robert Devine took control of the Stoughton Police Explorer's Class on or about 2002


and changed the program model from that of a police explorer's scouting program to that of a


quasi-paramilitary program that centered on teaching aspects of policing to youth participants. It


was in this program that Devine met Matthew and William Farwell.


        The Farwell brothers were known to have had some difficulties and disciplinary issues


 while attending school. Both embraced the Explorer's program with vigor and participated in all


 aspects of the program. Both eventually left alternative education and entered military service.


 56
       Matthew Farwell was appointed to the Wellesley Police Department in September 8,


2015. He transferred to the Stoughton Police Department by way of a lateral transfer on February


27, 2012.


       William Farwell was bypassed for employment on Scptember 6, 2 0 1 1 . In 2014, he


received an offer of employment for the position of patrol officer. He then requested and


received a military deferment under the US SERA Act. He had also received an appointment to


the Massachusetts State Police and briefly attended the MSP recruit academy. He was eventually


appointed to the Stoughton Police Department on March 27, 2017.


       The Farwell bothers returned to the Explorer's program as instructors. Matthew Farwell


met Sandra Birchmore while she was a participant in this program and was thirteen years of age


at the time. Matthew Farwell bega                         elationship with Sandra Birchmore.

       After a review of the personnel file of Robert Devine, I located two letters. One letter is

running the police Explorers program, The second letter is not dated or signed but titled "My


Hero Lieutenant Devine" and is a musing to Devine for all that he does for the community


[Exhibit 32). I have entered these as exhibits that exemplify both the public trust that was


violated and what the Stoughton Police Explorers Class was supposed to be.


       On January 24, 2016, Robert Devine entered into an agreement for discipline between the


Town and an employee, following the investigation that was conducted by Paul White. On


February 12, 2016, Civil Service form 10 was completed in where Devine was reinstated from


the position of non-civil service Deputy Chief, to his former Civil Service position of Police


Lieutenant. Civil Service form 1 1 - 1 0 was completed for the issuance of a demotion from

suspension on April 12, 2016.


       In the internal affairs file for Robert Devine, the agreement for the imposition of

that he understands it and is entering into it of his own free will andfurther that he understands


that future instances of him misusing his position or engaging in conduct unbecoming a police


officer or other misconduct may result in more serious disciplinary action being taken against


him, up to and including termination from his employment.


       The investigation by Paul White contained a finding that Robert Devine was not a

Of these reports, certain information has been redacted pursuant to G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (c) as this
information constitutes either medical information or personal and highly intimate details which if
disclosed would constitute an unwarranted invasion of the deceased’s and/or third-parties’ privacy. See
G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26)(c) (“personnel and medical files or information; also any other materials or data
relating to a specifically named individual, the disclosure of which may constitute an unwarranted
invasion of personal privacy”). Third-party civilian names have been withheld at this time pursuant to
G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26)(f) (investigatory exemption) as disclosure of their identities would have a chilling
effect and discourage “individual citizens to come forward and speak freely with police concerning
matters under investigation.” Bougas v. Chief of Police of Lexington, 371 Mass. 59, 62 (1976). Any
references to an underage sexual encounter, which on its face would appear to constitute statutory rape,
have been withheld under G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26)(a) (“specifically or by necessary implication exempted from
disclosure by statute”); G.L. c. 41, §97D (all reports of rape and sexual assault or attempts to commit such
offenses shall be maintained as confidential).
David Bae, Esq.
May 16, 2023
pg. 3

Personal messages of the deceased, Sandra Birchmore, which were obtained from her personal cellular
phone and laptop, contain highly personal and intimate details, including sexually explicit content and are
subject to the NDAO’s criminal investigation. Accordingly, these messages have been withheld under the
following statutory exemptions: G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26)(f) (investigatory exemption) and G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26)(c).

faster than the actual time.” The DVR system captured video upon detecting motion, therefore, these are
the full responsive video clips within our possession.

further surveillance than what is enclosed with this letter. Additionally, Matthew Farwell’s cell phone
records are nonresponsive because no relevant information regarding this investigation were found. See

Re: Public Records Request - Second Supplemental Response (SPR21/2518)

Dear Ms. Crimaldi:

On August 20, 2021, the Norfolk District Attorney’s Office (“NDAO”) provided a timely response
to your August 6, 2021 public records request for “a copy of the records concerning the
investigation into the death of [named individual] in Canton on Feb. 4, 2021.” You appealed the
NDAO’s response to the Supervisor of Public Records. On September 10, 2021, the Supervisor
of Records contacted the NDAO inquiring as to whether the NDAO would be willing to provide a
supplemental response explaining how the disclosure of the NDAO’s investigative materials
concerning the death of [named individual] would prejudice the Stoughton Police Department’s
internal affairs police investigation. The NDAO agreed to provide a supplemental response. On
September 24, 2021, the NDAO provided its supplemental response. On September 29, 2021, you
appealed the NDAO’s supplemental response to the Supervisor of Public Records. On October
14, 2021, the Supervisor of Public Records issued her determination, finding the NDAO “did not
meet its burden in demonstrating how disclosure of any segregable portion of the records would
probably so prejudice the possibility of effective law enforcement that such disclosure would not
be in the public interest.” The NDAO was ordered to provide you a supplemental response within
ten (10) business days.

These records have been subject to previous appeals involving both the NDAO and the Stoughton
Police Department.1 On July 14, 2021, after an in camera review, the Supervisor of Records
determined that the Stoughton Police Department may withhold records related to this named
individual as well as records related to a named police officer pursuant to G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (f).
See SPR21/1220. On August 10, 2021, the NDAO participated in an in camera review telephone
conversation with a staff attorney of the Public Records Division. During this in camera telephone
conversation, the NDAO explained the sensitive nature of the investigation and how the disclosure
of said materials would jeopardize the NDAO’s and Stoughton Police Department’s investigations.
On August 10, 2021, the Supervisor of Records issued a determination that the NDAO may
withhold the requested records under G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (f). Thereafter, the NDAO’s investigation
of the death of the [named individual] concluded. As a result of this investigation, however, the
NDAO provided Stoughton Police Department copies of its investigative materials related to the
death of the [named individual] as these materials were relevant to Stoughton Police Department’s

1
    See SPR21/0812; SPR21/1220; SPR21/1139; SPR21/0846; SPR21/2185.
open and active internal affairs police investigation. While the NDAO maintains it has met its
burden through its previous in camera review and subsequent responses, the NDAO supplements
its prior responses with the following information.

On October 19, 2021, counsel for Stoughton Police Department confirmed that the internal affairs
investigation is active and ongoing; that the department is actively reviewing its investigative
materials and it anticipates conducting interviews related to this investigation in December 2021.
Stoughton Police Deputy Chief Brian Holmes – through counsel - confirmed that the premature
release of any portion of these records would so jeopardize Stoughton Police Department’s internal
investigation that such disclosure is not in the public interest. Of particular concern, where
interviews have not yet occurred, but are anticipated to begin in the near future, disclosure of any
records related to this investigation would alert individual subject(s) of the investigation to the
activities of investigators and the scope of the investigation. Disclosure of the materials prior to
these interviews could also create a chilling effect and dissuade witnesses from coming forward to
report misconduct. See Bougas v. Chief of Police of Lexington, 371 Mass. 59, 62 (1976) (purposes
of investigatory exemption include “premature disclosure of the Commonwealth's case prior to
trial, the prevention of the disclosure of confidential investigative techniques, procedures, or
sources of information, the encouragement of individual citizens to come forward and speak freely
with police concerning matters under investigation, and the creation of initiative that police
officers might be completely candid in recording their observations, hypotheses and interim
conclusions”). The NDAO also cannot at this time confirm the records in its possession because
such confirmation would reveal the focus of Stoughton Police Department’s internal investigation
and alert certain individuals to the information in investigative officials’ possession. For the same
reasons, the NDAO cannot provide redacted copies of the investigative materials at this time.
Therefore, while the NDAO’s investigation has since concluded, the materials remain subject to
G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (f) because the disclosure of said materials would so prejudice the Stoughton
Police Department’s investigation that disclosure of said materials is not presently in the public
interest. See Continental Assurance Co. v. Diorio-Volungis, 51 Mass. App. Ct. 403, 411-413
(2001); WBZ-TV 4 v. District Attorney for the Suffolk District, 408 Mass. 595, 603 (1990).

Contrary to your suggestion in your September 29, 2021 letter of appeal, materials related to a
police department’s active internal affairs investigation may be withheld under the investigatory
exemption as these materials constitute “investigatory materials necessarily compiled out of the
public view” and such an investigation could result in disciplinary or criminal action. See Globe
Newspaper Co. v. Police Commr. of Boston, 419 Mass. 852, 859 n.10 (2004)(materials compiled
for internal affairs investigation covered by investigatory exemption); Worcester Telegram &
Gazette Corp. v. Chief of Police of Worcester, 58 Mass. App. Ct. 1, 7607 (2003)(“[T]he internal
affairs process exists specifically to address complaints of police corruption (theft, bribery,
acceptance of gratuities), misconduct (verbal and physical abuse, unlawful arrest, harassment), and
other criminal acts that would undermine the relationship of trust and confidence between the
police and the citizenry that is essential to law enforcement.”). In certain cases, premature
disclosure of investigative materials related to an internal affairs police investigation is not in the
public interest as it could prevent law enforcement officials from thoroughly and effectively
investigating police misconduct and in turn, taking appropriate disciplinary action. As set out
above, this is the case here.2

Please be advised you have a right to appeal this response to the Supervisor of Records. See G.L.
c. 66, § 10A.

                                              Meagen K. Monahan
                                              Meagen K. Monahan

2
  To the extent materials responsive to this request may eventually be released under the public
records law, such materials would still be subject to redaction or may be withheld in their entirety
in accordance with the public records law. See G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (f); G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (c)
(“personnel and medical files or information; also any other materials or data relating to a
specifically named individual, the disclosure of which may constitute an unwarranted invasion of
personal privacy”); and G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (a) (“specifically or by necessary implication exempted
from disclosure by statute”).

Dear Globe Readers


                                                                                                          2
August 26, 2021

Dear Supervisor,

I wish to appeal the August 20, 2021 response (the “Response”) of the Norfolk District
Attorney’s Office (the “Department”) to my August 6, 2021 public records request (the
“Request”) because I do not believe that the Response complies with the requirements of the
Massachusetts Public Records Law. G. L. c. 66, § 10.

I requested a “copy of the records concerning the investigation into the death of Sandra
Birchmore in Canton on Feb. 4, 2021.” The Department responded by declining to produce any
records, asserting that all of the requested records are entirely exempt pursuant to Exemption
(f). It also declined to “confirm the records in its possession,” despite the legal requirement that
it do so. G.L. c. 66, § 10(b)(iv). The Department acknowledges that its own investigation into
the death of Sandra Birchmore has concluded, and relies exclusively on the “Stoughton Police
Department’s internal investigation related to this matter” which the Department asserts is
“active and ongoing.”

Exemption (f) makes exempt “investigatory materials necessarily compiled out of public view by
law enforcement or other investigatory officials the disclosure of which materials would probably
so prejudice the possibility of effective law enforcement that such disclosure would not be in the
public interest.” G. L. c. 4, § 7(26)(f). The Department asserts that the Chief of the Stoughton
Police Department has informed that Department that “release of records responsive to your
request would jeopardize Stoughton Police Department’s active and ongoing investigation. As
such, the records you seek are exempt from public disclosure at this time pursuant to”
Exemption (f). This assertion falls far short of meeting the Department’s burden. Reinstein v.
Police Comm’r of Boston, 378 Mass. 281, 289-90 (1979)(the statutory exemptions are narrowly
construed and are not blanket in nature).

First, the Department refers to an “internal investigation related to this matter” by the Stoughton
Police Department. (emphasis added). It is not clear that an internal investigation constitutes
the type of “law enforcement” contemplated by the statute. Second, even if the Stoughton
Police Department’s internal matter constituted “law enforcement,” the Department has not
explained why the release of its records would “so prejudice the possibility of effective law
enforcement that disclosure would not be in the public interest.” Exemption (f) invites a “case-
by-case consideration” of whether disclosure “would probably so prejudice the possibility of
effective law enforcement that such disclosure would not be in the public interest.” See
Reinstein, 378 Mass. at 289-90. The Department has not even attempted such an analysis
here, instead relying on a statement by a third party. Third, even if some portion of the records


            1 Exchange Place, Suite 201 | Boston, MA 02109-2132 | 617.929.2000 | Globe.com
were exempt, any non-exempt, segregable portion of a public record is subject to mandatory
disclosure. G. L. c. 66, § 10(a).

Notably, the Department suggests that SPR21/1220 and SPR21/1139 are relevant to the
analysis here. However, in neither Order did the Supervisor determine that all records related to
the investigation of Ms. Birchmore’s death were exempt. Moreover, at the time of the orders,
there were active law enforcement investigations by both the Department and the

August 26, 2021

Dear Supervisor,

I wish to appeal the August 20, 2021 response (the “Response”) of the Norfolk District
Attorney’s Office (the “Department”) to my August 6, 2021 public records request (the
“Request”) because I do not believe that the Response complies with the requirements of the
Massachusetts Public Records Law. G. L. c. 66, § 10.

I requested a “copy of the records concerning the investigation into the death of Sandra
Birchmore in Canton on Feb. 4, 2021.” The Department responded by declining to produce any
records, asserting that all of the requested records are entirely exempt pursuant to Exemption
(f). It also declined to “confirm the records in its possession,” despite the legal requirement that
it do so. G.L. c. 66, § 10(b)(iv). The Department acknowledges that its own investigation into
the death of Sandra Birchmore has concluded, and relies exclusively on the “Stoughton Police
Department’s internal investigation related to this matter” which the Department asserts is
“active and ongoing.”

Exemption (f) makes exempt “investigatory materials necessarily compiled out of public view by
law enforcement or other investigatory officials the disclosure of which materials would probably
so prejudice the possibility of effective law enforcement that such disclosure would not be in the
public interest.” G. L. c. 4, § 7(26)(f). The Department asserts that the Chief of the Stoughton
Police Department has informed that Department that “release of records responsive to your
request would jeopardize Stoughton Police Department’s active and ongoing investigation. As
such, the records you seek are exempt from public disclosure at this time pursuant to”
Exemption (f). This assertion falls far short of meeting the Department’s burden. Reinstein v.
Police Comm’r of Boston, 378 Mass. 281, 289-90 (1979)(the statutory exemptions are narrowly
construed and are not blanket in nature).

First, the Department refers to an “internal investigation related to this matter” by the Stoughton
Police Department. (emphasis added). It is not clear that an internal investigation constitutes
the type of “law enforcement” contemplated by the statute. Second, even if the Stoughton
Police Department’s internal matter constituted “law enforcement,” the Department has not
explained why the release of its records would “so prejudice the possibility of effective law
enforcement that disclosure would not be in the public interest.” Exemption (f) invites a “case-
by-case consideration” of whether disclosure “would probably so prejudice the possibility of
effective law enforcement that such disclosure would not be in the public interest.” See
Reinstein, 378 Mass. at 289-90. The Department has not even attempted such an analysis
here, instead relying on a statement by a third party. Third, even if some portion of the records


            1 Exchange Place, Suite 201 | Boston, MA 02109-2132 | 617.929.2000 | Globe.com
were exempt, any non-exempt, segregable portion of a public record is subject to mandatory
disclosure. G. L. c. 66, § 10(a).

Notably, the Department suggests that SPR21/1220 and SPR21/1139 are relevant to the
analysis here. However, in neither Order did the Supervisor determine that all records related to
the investigation of Ms. Birchmore’s death were exempt. Moreover, at the time of the orders,
there were active law enforcement investigations by both the Department and the
Massachusetts State Police, in addition to the internal affairs investigation in Stoughton. The
law enforcement investigations have since concluded, which means that the applicability of
Exemption (f) must be reassessed. In fact, in SPR21/1139 the Supervisor specifically noted that
“a change in the status of the investigation may change the applicability of Exemption (f) to
these records.”

I respectfully request that the Supervisor order the Department to, within ten business days,
clarify what records are in its possession and produce the records for which it has failed to meet
its burden.

Laura Crimaldi

Sept. 29, 2021

Dear Supervisor,

I wish to appeal the September 24, 2021 Supplemental Response of the Norfolk District
Attorney’s Office (the “Department”) to my public records request and to the Supervisor’s
Order. SPR21/2185. I requested “a copy of the records concerning the investigation into the
death of Sandra Birchmore in Canton on February 4, 2021.” These records have been the subject
of previous appeals, though the Supervisor’s previous orders were issued before the conclusion
of the Norfolk District Attorney’s Office’s law enforcement investigation. The only remaining
investigation is an internal affairs one by the Stoughton Police Department.

Exemption (f) permits the withholding of “investigatory materials necessarily compiled out of
the public view by law enforcement or other investigatory officials the disclosure of which
materials would probably so prejudice the possibility of effective law enforcement that such
disclosure would not be in the public interest.” G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26)(f) (emphasis added). In order
for Exemption (f) to apply here, the disclosure of materials would have to be so harmful to the
Stoughton Police Department’s internal affairs investigation that the Police Department or some
other law enforcement entity would be prejudiced in its ability to effectively enforce the law.
See generally Rahim v. District Att’y for Suffolk Dist., 486 Mass. 544, 551 (2020) (“Depending
on the contents of a particular record, exemption (f) may cover only certain aspects of the
record[.]”) Even if the Department could support the argument that disclosure of the records
would prejudice the Stoughton Police Department’s ability to appropriately assess and discipline
its employee as part of its internal affairs investigation, which the Department has not done, that
would not be enough. The relevant prejudice is to the enforcement of the law.

As a general matter, courts have held that making internal affairs files public under the public
records law is appropriate and in the public interest. See Worcester Telegram & Gazette Corp. v.
Chief of Police of Worcester, Mass. App. Ct. 1, 8–9, 787 N.E.2d 602, 608 (2003) (noting, in the
context of Exemption (c), which is not at issue here, that “[i]t would be odd, indeed, to shield
from the light of public scrutiny as ‘personnel [file] or information’ the workings and
determinations of a process whose quintessential purpose is to inspire public confidence.”). As
in Worcester, it would be odd to withhold internal affairs documents on the grounds that
disclosure would “so prejudice the possibility of effective law enforcement that disclosure would
not be in the public interest.” G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26)(f).


            1 Exchange Place, Suite 201 | Boston, MA 02109-2132 | 617.929.2000 | Globe.com
The cases cited by the Department in purported support of its claim that “while the NDAO’s
investigation has since concluded, the materials remain subject to” Exemption (f) because of the
ongoing internal affairs investigation by the Stoughton Police Department are distinguishable
from the case at hand because both involved ongoing criminal investigations. In Continental
Assurance Co. v. Diorio-Volungis, the Appeals Court held that the lower court had not been
required to conduct an in camera review of records to determine that Exemption (f) applied,
because sufficient testimony existed “to support the judge's conclusion that [the homicide]
investigation was ongoing, that the police had not disclosed investigation information to the
press, and that disclosure would prejudice the open investigation.” 51 Mass. App. Ct. 403, 411-
413 (2001). Similarly, in WBZ-TV 4 v. District Attorney for the Suffolk District, the Supreme
Judicial Court determined that a tape recorded statement and video line up could be withheld
because of an ongoing criminal investigation. 408 Mass. 595, 603 (1990). There, the court
“emphasize[d] . . . that nondisclosure is specific to the circumstances of the ongoing criminal
investigation at this time and that in the future disclosure may be appropriate.”

In assessing whether disclosure of the public records at issue here “would so prejudice the
possibility of effective law enforcement that such disclosure would not be in the public interest,”
the strength of the public interest is also relevant. It is not uncommon for internal affairs
investigations to go on for many years. The public has a strong interest in not waiting for the
Department to conclude its investigation, when that could mean years without these important
records being made available.

In permitting the Stoughton Police Department to withhold the records at issue here back in July,
your office noted, “[p]lease be aware that a change in the status of the investigation could impact
the applicability of Exemption (f).” (SPR21/1220). The status of the law enforcement
investigation by the Norfolk District’s Attorney’s Office has changed and I respectfully request
that you order the Department to produce the requested records. See generally Gatehouse Media,
LLC v. City of Worcester, No. 1885CV1526A, 2021 WL 2328416, at * (Worcester Superior
Court June 2, 2021) (finding justification for redactions of ongoing internal affairs files
insufficient and ordering counsel for both parties to have access to the documents subject to an
appropriate protective order in order to assist the court in determining whether the redactions
were warranted).


Laura Crimaldi
Reporter

Re: Public Records Request - Second Supplemental Response (SPR21/2518)

Dear Ms. Crimaldi:

On August 20, 2021, the Norfolk District Attorney’s Office (“NDAO”) provided a timely response
to your August 6, 2021 public records request for “a copy of the records concerning the
investigation into the death of [named individual] in Canton on Feb. 4, 2021.” You appealed the
NDAO’s response to the Supervisor of Public Records. On September 10, 2021, the Supervisor
of Records contacted the NDAO inquiring as to whether the NDAO would be willing to provide a
supplemental response explaining how the disclosure of the NDAO’s investigative materials
concerning the death of [named individual] would prejudice the Stoughton Police Department’s
internal affairs police investigation. The NDAO agreed to provide a supplemental response. On
September 24, 2021, the NDAO provided its supplemental response. On September 29, 2021, you
appealed the NDAO’s supplemental response to the Supervisor of Public Records. On October
14, 2021, the Supervisor of Public Records issued her determination, finding the NDAO “did not
meet its burden in demonstrating how disclosure of any segregable portion of the records would
probably so prejudice the possibility of effective law enforcement that such disclosure would not
be in the public interest.” The NDAO was ordered to provide you a supplemental response within
ten (10) business days.

These records have been subject to previous appeals involving both the NDAO and the Stoughton
Police Department.1 On July 14, 2021, after an in camera review, the Supervisor of Records
determined that the Stoughton Police Department may withhold records related to this named
individual as well as records related to a named police officer pursuant to G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (f).
See SPR21/1220. On August 10, 2021, the NDAO participated in an in camera review telephone
conversation with a staff attorney of the Public Records Division. During this in camera telephone
conversation, the NDAO explained the sensitive nature of the investigation and how the disclosure
of said materials would jeopardize the NDAO’s and Stoughton Police Department’s investigations.
On August 10, 2021, the Supervisor of Records issued a determination that the NDAO may
withhold the requested records under G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (f). Thereafter, the NDAO’s investigation
of the death of the [named individual] concluded. As a result of this investigation, however, the
NDAO provided Stoughton Police Department copies of its investigative materials related to the
death of the [named individual] as these materials were relevant to Stoughton Police Department’s

1
    See SPR21/0812; SPR21/1220; SPR21/1139; SPR21/0846; SPR21/2185.
open and active internal affairs police investigation. While the NDAO maintains it has met its
burden through its previous in camera review and subsequent responses, the NDAO supplements
its prior responses with the following information.

On October 19, 2021, counsel for Stoughton Police Department confirmed that the internal affairs
investigation is active and ongoing; that the department is actively reviewing its investigative
materials and it anticipates conducting interviews related to this investigation in December 2021.
Stoughton Police Deputy Chief Brian Holmes – through counsel - confirmed that the premature
release of any portion of these records would so jeopardize Stoughton Police Department’s internal
investigation that such disclosure is not in the public interest. Of particular concern, where
interviews have not yet occurred, but are anticipated to begin in the near future, disclosure of any
records related to this investigation would alert individual subject(s) of the investigation to the
activities of investigators and the scope of the investigation. Disclosure of the materials prior to
these interviews could also create a chilling effect and dissuade witnesses from coming forward to
report misconduct. See Bougas v. Chief of Police of Lexington, 371 Mass. 59, 62 (1976) (purposes
of investigatory exemption include “premature disclosure of the Commonwealth's case prior to
trial, the prevention of the disclosure of confidential investigative techniques, procedures, or
sources of information, the encouragement of individual citizens to come forward and speak freely
with police concerning matters under investigation, and the creation of initiative that police
officers might be completely candid in recording their observations, hypotheses and interim
conclusions”). The NDAO also cannot at this time confirm the records in its possession because
such confirmation would reveal the focus of Stoughton Police Department’s internal investigation
and alert certain individuals to the information in investigative officials’ possession. For the same
reasons, the NDAO cannot provide redacted copies of the investigative materials at this time.
Therefore, while the NDAO’s investigation has since concluded, the materials remain subject to
G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26) (f) because the disclosure of said materials would so prejudice the Stoughton
Police Department’s investigation that disclosure of said materials is not presently in the public
interest. See Continental Assurance Co. v. Diorio-Volungis, 51 Mass. App. Ct. 403, 411-413
(2001); WBZ-TV 4 v. District Attorney for the Suffolk District, 408 Mass. 595, 603 (1990).

Contrary to your suggestion in your September 29, 2021 letter of appeal, materials related to a
police department’s active internal affairs investigation may be withheld under the investigatory
exemption as these materials constitute “investigatory materials necessarily compiled out of the
public view” and such an investigation could result in disciplinary or criminal action. See Globe
Newspaper Co. v. Police Commr. of Boston, 419 Mass. 852, 859 n.10 (2004)(materials compiled
for internal affairs investigation covered by investigatory exemption); Worcester Telegram &
Gazette Corp. v. Chief of Police of Worcester, 58 Mass. App. Ct. 1, 7607 (2003)(“[T]he internal
affairs process exists specifically to address complaints of police corruption (theft, bribery,
acceptance of gratuities), misconduct (verbal and physical abuse, unlawful arrest, harassment), and
other criminal acts that would undermine the relationship of trust and confidence between the
police and the citizenry that is essential to law enforcement.”). In certain cases, premature
disclosure of investigative materials related to an internal affairs police investigation is not in the
public interest as it could prevent law enforcement officials from thoroughly and effectively
investigating police misconduct and in turn, taking appropriate disciplinary action. As set out
above, this is the case here.2

Please be advised you have a right to appeal this response to the Supervisor of Records. See G.L.
c. 66, § 10A.

Dear Supervisor,

I wish to appeal the October 28, 2021 Second Supplemental Response of the Norfolk District
Attorney’s Office (the “Department”) to my public records request and to the Supervisor’s
Orders. SPR21/2185. I requested “a copy of the records concerning the investigation into the
death of Sandra Birchmore in Canton on February 4, 2021.” These records have been the subject
of multiple previous appeals.

The Department continues to assert, solely on the basis of Exemption (f), that it cannot produce
any redacted records, or even meet its burden under G.L. c. 66, § 10(b)(iv) to identify which
records are in its possession. Exemption (f) permits the withholding of “investigatory materials
necessarily compiled out of the public view by law enforcement or other investigatory officials
the disclosure of which materials would probably so prejudice the possibility of effective law
enforcement that such disclosure would not be in the public interest.” G.L. c. 4, § 7 (26)(f)
(emphasis added). Neither Exemption (f) nor any other exemption creates an exception to the
requirement that a Department “identify any records, categories of records or portions of records
that the agency or municipality intends to withhold.” G.L. c. 66, § 10(b)(iv).

The Department’s argument is based on the purported impact that release of the records would
have on the Stoughton Police Department’s internal investigation. Specifically, the Department
cites (i) the Stoughton Police Deputy Chief’s personal opinion that release of the materials would
jeopardize the Police Department’s investigation, (ii) concern that “where interviews have not
yet occurred, but are anticipated to begin in the near future, disclosure of any records related to
this investigation would alert individual subject(s) of the investigation to the activities of
investigators and the scope of the investigation,” and (iii) concern that “[d]isclosure of the
materials prior to these interviews could also create a chilling effect and dissuade witnesses from
coming forward to report misconduct.” The Deputy Chief’s personal opinion does not meet the
Department’s legal burden to show that an exemption applies. Similarly, it is unclear why every
single record must be entirely withheld (and not even identified) in order to avoid individual
subjects learning the scope of the investigation in a manner that “so prejudices effective law
enforcement that disclosure is not in the public interest.” It is also unclear whether the
Department’s argument is meant to suggest that it will be able to produce the records after the


            1 Exchange Place, Suite 201 | Boston, MA 02109-2132 | 617.929.2000 | Globe.com
interviews occur in December of 2021. Finally, it is unclear why records cannot be redacted and
produced in a manner that avoids creating a chilling effect on any voluntary witnesses.

I respectfully request that the Department be required, within 10 business days, to (1) identify
any records, categories of records or portions of records responsive to the request and in its
possession, and (2) produce the records for which it still has not met its burden under Exemption
(f), redacted where necessary.

Sincerely,

Laura Crimaldi

Reporter


             1 Exchange Place, Suite 201 | Boston, MA 02109-2132 | 617.929.2000 | Globe.com

backlash
President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine has signed into law three
measures aimed at replenishing the ranks of his country’s exhausted and
battered army, including the politically poisonous step of lowering the
age when men become eligible for mobilization, and eliminating some
medical exemptions. Continue reading →

WORLD

Taiwan’s strongest earthquake in 25 years kills 9 and
injures hundreds
The first quake was alarming enough — a rumble more powerful than
anything felt in Taiwan for a quarter-century, lasting for more than a
minute on Wednesday morning, knocking belongings and even whole
buildings askew. It was so strong it set off tsunami warnings in Japan,
China, and the Philippines. Continue reading →

alliance was poised to take more control over military support sent to
Ukraine — a role that the United States has played for the past two years.
